venues.d: The city's defining luxury address — a serene cliffside villa terraced above the Adriatic, every room facing Lokrum island and the walled city beyond.
A 1913 grande dame on the Ploče waterfront, five minutes' walk from the city walls — the most enviable address in Dubrovnik proper.
A full seafront resort in Mediterranean gardens — three pools, a private beach and a large spa, the region's most complete address for families.
A polished cliffside five-star cascading down terraced slopes to the water, about a mile from the walled city — sleek rooms, sea views and a large spa.
A restored 1930s villa of just thirteen rooms above the Adriatic — art-filled, intimate and steps from the Old Town, with a private bathing platform below.

venues.a: Old Town (Stari Grad, on the ramparts)
venues.d: Dubrovnik's only MICHELIN star — chef Marijo Curić's refined Mediterranean cooking on a terrace built into the medieval walls above the old harbour.
Dubrovnik's grand classic — traditional Dalmatian cooking on French and Italian foundations, on terraces facing the illuminated Lovrijenac and Bokar fortresses.
The elegant table at Villa Dubrovnik — chef Robert Račić's regional, seasonal cooking with Adriatic seafood at its heart, on a cliffside terrace.
A rooftop room atop a 500-year-old palace on Prijeko street — modern Mediterranean cooking above the terracotta roofs of the walled city.
A romantic rooftop hidden above the old town's lanes — refined, contemporary cooking and one of the quieter fine-dining rooms inside the walls.
A Dubrovnik institution since 1886 — fresh Adriatic fish and shellfish done simply and well, with a leafy first-floor terrace above the old town.

venues.a: Old Town (Bošković Square, by St Ignatius)
venues.d: A quiet square-side table reviving old Dubrovnik recipes — the signature is capon (kopun), slow-baked in the traditional way.
A relaxed modern bistro in Lapad — slow-cooked, market-led Dalmatian cooking (the name means 'fork' in the local dialect) at honest value.
A small room in a quiet corner of the walled city marrying Mediterranean produce with Asian technique — Dubrovnik's most distinctive fusion table.
Not Indian despite the name — a warm, unpretentious room serving Bosnian home cooking and grilled meats in the heart of the walls.

The essential Dubrovnik experience: a near-2km circuit atop 13th-century ramparts, 25 metres above the sea, looking down on the terracotta rooftops and out to Lokrum. Go early or at golden hour when the crowds thin and the light turns the stone honey-gold; a private guide can pace it for grandparents and children alike.

The limestone-paved main promenade, polished to a mirror shine by centuries of footsteps, runs the length of the walled city from Pile to Ploče. It is where Dubrovnik takes its evening passeggiata — a glass of wine at a pavement table as the marble glows under the lamps.

The two grand fortified entrances to the walled city, each with a wooden drawbridge and a niche holding a statue of St Blaise, the city's patron. Passing through Pile onto the Stradun is the classic first-arrival moment — arrange to enter on foot with a guide rather than in the cruise-crowd crush.

A great domed 16th-century fountain just inside Pile Gate, the endpoint of a 12km aqueduct built in 1438 — water still runs from its sixteen carved mascarons. A cool, shaded meeting point and a lovely first landmark for children to spot.

Home to one of the oldest working pharmacies in Europe, founded in 1317, alongside a serene Romanesque cloister of double columns and a museum of medieval apothecary jars. The pharmacy still compounds creams to centuries-old Franciscan recipes — a quiet, cultured pause off the busy Stradun.

The Gothic-Renaissance seat of the Ragusan Republic, whose rector governed for a single month and could not leave the building during his term. Now the Cultural History Museum, its courtyard has flawless acoustics and hosts summer chamber concerts — a refined evening for a multi-generational party.

A serene Baroque cathedral built after the 1667 earthquake, holding paintings by Italian and Dalmatian masters. Its Treasury is the draw — reliquaries of gold and silver, including the jewelled skull-reliquary of St Blaise and a relic said to be a fragment of the True Cross.

Tucked by the Ploče gate, a fortress-like 14th-century monastery with a luminous late-Gothic cloister and a museum of Dubrovnik-school painting, including an altarpiece attributed to Titian. Calmer than the Franciscan cloister and a favourite for those who like art without the crowds.

The finest surviving pre-earthquake palace, a Gothic-Renaissance jewel on Luža Square that served as the Republic's mint and customs house. It now guards the State Archives, and its arcaded courtyard is one of the coolest, most photogenic spots to step out of the sun.

venues.n: Luža Square, Orlando's Column & the Bell Tower
venues.d: The ceremonial heart of the old city: the medieval Orlando's Column (its forearm was the Republic's official measure of length), the 15th-century Bell Tower with its bronze 'green men' who strike the hour, and the Church of St Blaise. The natural place to sit with a coffee and watch the city move.

A 16th-century grain silo whose vast underground pits ('rupe' means holes) kept the Republic fed through any siege, now a folk-life museum of Konavle costume and craft. Cool, quiet and unusual — and a Game of Thrones location for those who care to know it stood in for a King's Landing street.

A powerful, world-class photojournalism gallery on Antuninska street, just off the Stradun, founded to show the human reality of conflict — the Balkan wars and beyond. Sobering and beautifully curated; a serious counterpoint to the city's beauty, best for adults and older teens.

venues.n: Maritime Museum & Aquarium at Fort St John
venues.d: Inside the sea-facing Fort St John, the Maritime Museum tells Dubrovnik's story as a great trading republic through ship models and charts, with a small aquarium of Adriatic sea life on the ground floor. An easy, engaging stop that works well for children.

A sweeping Baroque staircase — Dubrovnik's own 'Spanish Steps' — climbing to the elegant Jesuit church of St Ignatius on the city's highest terrace. A quiet, handsome corner of the old town, and famous as the site of Cersei's walk of shame.

The intimate historic harbour beneath the eastern walls, ringed by the arsenal arches where the Republic once built its galleys. Wooden boats bob against the stone; it is the departure point for Lokrum and island trips, and a lovely spot for an early-evening aperitivo.

The dramatic 'Gibraltar of Dubrovnik', a triangular fortress perched on a 37-metre sea-cliff just outside the walls, inscribed above its gate: 'Freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world.' Fans will know it as the Red Keep; everyone else comes for the finest view back onto the walled city.

venues.n: Cable car up Mount Srđ & Fort Imperial
venues.d: A four-minute glide 412 metres up to the ridge behind the city, where the whole walled town, Lokrum and the Elaphiti Islands lay spread below. Time it for sunset with a table at the summit restaurant — one of the great panoramas of the Adriatic, effortless for grandparents.

venues.n: Museum of the Homeland War, Fort Imperial
venues.d: Inside Napoleon's hilltop Fort Imperial — the first line of defence during the 1991–95 siege — an exhibition of documents, weapons and film that explains how the city held. Moving and important context, paired naturally with the cable-car ascent and the summit views.

venues.n: Sunset drinks at a Buža bar
venues.d: Slip through a literal hole in the sea walls ('buža' means hole) to bare tables set on the bare rock, a cold drink in hand and nothing between you and Lokrum but the Adriatic. Unpretentious and unforgettable — the city's best-loved sundowner, cash only and worth every minute.

The pretty pebble beach just outside the Ploče gate, with the walled city as its backdrop — a beach club with loungers and a restaurant on one side, free shingle on the other. Convenient for a swim between sightseeing, with cabana service for those who prefer their sun shaded.

Paddle out from beneath Fort Lovrijenac around the walls and across to Lokrum, slipping into sea caves and a quiet cove for a swim along the way. A genuinely memorable half-day on the water — private guided outings can be arranged for families and set to an easy pace.

A ten-minute boat hop to a forested island of holm oak and cypress, with a botanical garden, a ruined Benedictine monastery, roaming peacocks and rabbits, and the salt 'Dead Sea' lagoon for a warm, buoyant swim. Car-free and shaded — a blissful, unhurried escape for all ages.

A short climb through Lokrum's woods to a star-shaped Napoleonic fort crowning the island, with a 360-degree panorama back to Dubrovnik's walls and out over the open Adriatic. A rewarding little adventure to pair with a lazy island afternoon.

venues.n: Private boat to the Elaphiti Islands
venues.d: A day on the water to the car-free trio of Koločep, Lopud and Šipan — swimming from a chartered yacht, lunching on grilled fish, wandering Lopud's Sunj sand beach and Šipan's olive groves and old sea-captains' mansions. The relaxed, glamorous way to see the archipelago, on your own schedule.

The most polished of the Elaphiti islands, car-free and green, ending in Šunj — one of the few genuine sand beaches near Dubrovnik, shallow and warm for children. A leafy promenade, a few good tavernas and a Renaissance monastery-turned-hotel make it a serene day out.

The largest and quietest Elaphiti island, where Ragusan nobles built summer villas among the olive groves and vineyards. Two sleepy harbour hamlets, a scattering of ruined palaces, and long lunches of just-caught fish — deep calm within an hour of the old town.

The nearest and greenest Elaphiti island, laced with pine paths and famous for its sea caves and the luminous Blue Cave, best entered by small boat or kayak. A gentle, unhurried spot for a swim and a seafood lunch far from the crowds.

A Renaissance nobleman's garden 20 minutes up the coast, the oldest arboretum in this part of the world, with a stone aqueduct, a Neptune fountain and 500-year-old plane trees framing Adriatic views. Fans will recognise it as the Red Keep gardens; gardeners simply love its serene terraces.

For the many who came to King's Landing before they came to Dubrovnik: the Jesuit Stairs of the walk of shame, Fort Lovrijenac as the Red Keep, the Ethnographic Museum Rupe, and the harbour and walls that framed a hundred scenes. A fun, well-guided way to read the old city through a different lens.

venues.n: Day trip: Ston walls & oysters, Pelješac
venues.d: An hour north, the little town of Ston guards Europe's longest medieval fortification — a 5km wall climbing the hillside — beside ancient salt pans still worked by hand. Then to neighbouring Mali Ston to shuck oysters straight from the beds where they grow; a perfect gourmet half-day, wine included.

The peninsula's steep, sun-baked slopes produce Croatia's boldest reds — the celebrated Dingač and Postup from the Plavac Mali grape. Private tastings at family cellars, long lunches with a sea view, and quiet coves for a swim; a grown-up, unhurried counterpoint to the walled city.

A gentle 20-minute boat south to a palm-lined Riviera town of yacht-filled harbour and easy waterfront tavernas — Dubrovnik's calmer, more elegant neighbour. Climb to the Račić family mausoleum, a masterpiece in white stone by the sculptor Ivan Meštrović, above the cypress cemetery.

The green, spring-fed valley south of the city, a patchwork of vineyards, water-mills and villages keeping the old crafts of silk embroidery and folk dance alive. A day of farm-table feasts, horse-riding and quiet back-roads — the authentic, rural Dalmatia most visitors never see.

venues.n: Day trip: Bay of Kotor, Montenegro
venues.d: Two hours south into the Mediterranean's only true fjord, its cliffs plunging to still water dotted with medieval towns. Wander walled Kotor, sail out to the man-made islet of Our Lady of the Rocks off Perast, and take in one of Europe's most dramatic coastlines — passports and a private driver make it seamless.

A longer day inland to the Ottoman crossroads of Mostar, where the soaring 16th-century Stari Most arches over the emerald Neretva — reconstructed stone by stone after the war, and still where local divers plunge from its parapet. A vivid, moving glimpse of a wholly different culture, bazaars and coppersmiths included.

In a converted graphite factory in the port district, Croatia's first museum of the socialist Yugoslav era — a recreated 1980s apartment, propaganda, design and everyday objects, told with wit rather than nostalgia. An offbeat, thought-provoking hour for the curious traveller.

The working port where locals actually shop — a morning market of Konavle figs, lavender, olive oil and just-landed fish along the quay. A refreshingly real, un-touristed corner, and the departure point for many island boats and yacht charters.

Learn to make Dalmatian classics — black risotto, peka slow-cooked under embers, fresh olive oil tasting — in a private class or at a Konavle farmstead. Chefs happily build vegetarian menus for Indian palates; a hands-on afternoon the whole family can share.

venues.n: Sunset cruise on a traditional gulet
venues.d: Charter a classic wooden gulet for the golden hour, gliding beneath the floodlit walls and around Lokrum with drinks and canapés on deck. Discreet, glamorous and easy — the quintessential Adriatic evening, tailored to a private group.

venues.n: Cabrio Sports Car & Buggy safari, Srđ
venues.d: For families with restless teenagers, a guided buggy or vintage-car run through the hills behind Dubrovnik, off the tourist grid to hidden viewpoints and old fortifications. A dose of adventure and open air with the whole city laid out below.

venues.n: Cathedral of the Assumption Bell & the Rupe views
venues.d: Climb to the upper lanes above the Stradun where washing lines stretch between shuttered houses and cats doze on warm stone — the lived-in Dubrovnik behind the monuments. A short, atmospheric wander that rewards those who leave the main drag for the steep side-streets.

A guided walk led by a Dubrovnik local who lived through the 1991–92 siege, reading the shell scars still visible on the paving and rooftops. Deeply human and quietly powerful — the story that turns a beautiful backdrop into a living city.

venues.n: Private evening in the Rector's Palace atrium
venues.d: During the summer festival the palace courtyard becomes a candlelit concert hall of near-perfect acoustics, staging chamber music and opera under the Adriatic stars. A rare, refined experience — arrange seats and a late dinner afterwards for a special-occasion night.
Dubrovnik's most famous drink — a cliff-ledge bar reached through a literal hole ('buža') in the city wall, with nothing between your table and the Adriatic.
The Old Town's best-loved wine bar — a knowledgeable, welcoming room pouring Croatian wines by the glass, ideal before or after dinner.
A cocktail on the terrace of Croatia's most decorated hotel — the walled city, Lokrum and the open Adriatic laid out below.
A cocktail bar set inside a natural sea cave — drinks under a floodlit limestone cavern with a glass floor over a pool of Adriatic water.
